title: TensorLUT
youtubeTitle: HELUT TensorLUT: Searching and Emitting Truth Tables
description: TensorLUT turns supported Yosys LUT truth tables into continuous search variables, evaluates them on Metal, and emits discrete Verilog only when bounded checks pass. A live proof ladder shows six implementation-level certificate checks; 2, 4, and 6 melted LUTs of an 8-LUT adder proving at one budget; all 8 returning a binary but wrong result at that budget; and the same 8-of-8 fixture proving with a larger budget. Analytic completeness remains narrow, while bounded SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two tables. This is not arbitrary-topology completeness and not a P1030680 decrypt. Epoch C71.

scenes.headline: TensorLUT
scenes.subhead: Search the truth tables, then demand discrete hardware.
scenes.voiceover: Another HELUT research path is TensorLUT. A look-up table normally has a fixed truth table, stored in a value called INIT. TensorLUT treats those entries as search variables, relaxes them to continuous values, and optimizes the circuit on Metal.

scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-06 · certificate plus bounded search fixtures
scenes.voiceover: Read this as two ladders. First, the formal certificate: six implementation-level checks for the objective, emitter, involution structure, and freeze mask. That is not a convergence theorem. Second, a fixed 4-bit adder. Erase 2 of its 8 tables and the searched circuit proves. Erase 4, it proves. Erase 6, it proves. Erase all 8 at the same 120-generation budget and it returns fully binary but wrong: REFUTED, fitness -16. Third screen, same full erase with 500 generations: PROVED. So the old sentence that evidence stops at two tables is no longer true. The analytic theorem stays narrow; end-to-end SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two. Arbitrary topology and guaranteed convergence remain open.

scenes.headline: Continuous search, binary destination
scenes.subhead: A six-input LUT has 64 truth-table entries.
scenes.voiceover: The cycle has four stages: melt, score, freeze, and snap. Melting means taking the 64 truth-table entries of a six-input look-up table and letting them hold fractional values, blending between entries instead of choosing. Scoring compares circuit output against target behavior. Freezing holds the parts that must not move. Snapping raises a penalty that pushes every entry back to zero or one, and only then does the emitter write a discrete Verilog circuit.

scenes.headline: What worked—and what did not
scenes.voiceover: To test this search on a real stateful circuit, I used an unmodified historical Enigma M4 netlist as one benchmark. It first serves as a zero-error baseline. Attempts to melt every entry, or only the plugboard cone, shattered: thousands of values refused to settle to zero or one. The current bounded experiment freezes the known circuit and searches only an involutive plugboard, meaning one that undoes itself, of at most ten swapped pairs. A blind three-pair recovery passed on a short crib.

scenes.headline: Continuous does not automatically mean discrete
scenes.subhead: The analytic result is narrow; SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two LUTs.
scenes.voiceover: The analytic result is bounded, and the boundary is precise. For one fully observed look-up table, there is a proof that it returns to its target truth table from anywhere inside the snap basin: the region where every entry is already nearer its goal than its opposite. A second certificate extends that analytic bridge to a two-table cascade and emits Verilog. That analytic completeness ladder still stops there. End-to-end evidence now goes farther: fixed ripple adders with 2, 4, and 6 of 8 tables melted prove; all 8 fail at the smaller budget and prove at 500 generations; and a 2-of-16 repair trained on 64 rows proves over all 65,536 inputs. Those are bounded deterministic fixtures, not arbitrary netlists or a convergence theorem.

scenes.headline: Related experiments are not interchangeable
bullets: TensorLUT does not supply a P1030680 crib
M4 application and E256 offshoot are distinct
No live cipher mutates without review
scenes.voiceover: That M4 benchmark does not turn TensorLUT into an Enigma project, and it is not evidence that P1030680 is broken. TensorLUT supplies no guessed plaintext, key, or decrypt. Searching a look-up-table genotype, searching historical M4 settings in a chosen application, and proposing a new E256 profile in a later offshoot are related experiments, but they are not the same process. None should mutate a live cipher without review.

scenes.headline: Next: one application—the P1030680 Bombe
scenes.subhead: Why choose Enigma? Then define cribs, inspect the machine, and bound the result.
scenes.voiceover: One separate application combined HELUT's cleartext compiler and TensorLUT machinery with a historical Enigma target. Next, I explain why I chose that problem, define the attack terms, and follow each stop through the candidate and break gates. The FHE work remains a separate research path.
